##  {#github-pages-what data-menu-title="What is GitHub Pages"}

[What is GitHub Pages?]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
GitHub Pages is a free hosting service that turns a GitHub repository
into a website.

-   Every repository can have its own site
-   The URL follows a predictable pattern
-   It updates every time you push to `main`
-   Works with any `.html` file — including Quarto output

**The key insight:** `index.html` is the default page. Whatever is in
`index.html` is what visitors see first.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#url-pattern data-menu-title="URL Pattern"}

[The URL pattern]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
GitHub follows a consistent naming convention:
:::

```         
https://{username}.github.io/{repo_name}/
```

::: body-text
**Examples:**

-   `github.com` → `github.io`
-   `github.com/gretchen/training_gretchen` becomes
    `gretchen.github.io/training_gretchen/`

**Chat prompt coming:** What would *your* GitHub Pages URL be?
:::

##  {#workflow-overview data-menu-title="Workflow Overview"}

[The publishing workflow]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
There are four steps, and you already know all of them:

1.  Create `index.qmd` at the root of your repo
2.  Render it → produces `index.html`
3.  Commit and push both files to GitHub
4.  Activate GitHub Pages in Settings → Pages

After step 4, every future push automatically updates your site. **No
extra steps.**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#index-qmd data-menu-title="index.qmd"}

[Why `index.qmd`?]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
`index.html` is a web convention — it's the "front door."

When a browser visits a folder (like your repo), it automatically looks
for `index.html` and serves it.

-   Name must be exactly `index` (lowercase)
-   Operating systems handle case differently — get this right
-   The corresponding `index.qmd` is what you edit
-   Render it to get `index.html`

If you also have an `index_files/` folder — commit that too.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#setup-steps data-menu-title="Setup Steps"}

[Setting up: step by step]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**In RStudio:**

1.  Open your `training_{USERNAME}` project
2.  `File → New File → Quarto Document`
3.  Title: "GitHub Pages Example", format: HTML
4.  Save as `index.qmd` at the **top level** of the project
5.  Click Render → observe `index.html` appears
6.  Commit both `index.qmd` and `index.html`, push

**On GitHub:**

7.  Settings → Pages
8.  Branch: change from "None" → `main`, folder: root
9.  Click Save
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#activating-pages data-menu-title="Activating Pages"}

[Activating GitHub Pages]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
After clicking Save you'll see:

> *"Your GitHub Pages site is currently being built from the main
> branch"*

**Wait 1–2 minutes**, then visit your URL.

If you don't see your page:

-   Check that `index.html` is committed and pushed
-   Check the URL exactly — trailing `/` matters
-   Hard refresh your browser (`Cmd+Shift+R` or `Ctrl+Shift+R`)
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#linking-files data-menu-title="Linking Files"}

[Linking multiple files]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
Your `index.qmd` can link to *any* other rendered `.html` file in your
repo using standard Markdown syntax:

``` markdown
[Data wrangling and cleaning](scripts/data-wrangling-cleaning.html)
```

The path is **relative** — it starts from where `index.qmd` lives.

**For this to work:**

-   The `.html` file must exist (render first)
-   The `.html` file must be committed and pushed
:::

##  {#what-makes-good-page data-menu-title="What Makes a Good Page"}

[What makes a good landing page?]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
Think about your audience.

**For an advisor or committee:**

-   Brief description of the project
-   Clear links to each analysis component
-   A note about the data source

**For a collaborator:**

-   What the repo contains
-   How to navigate the analyses
-   Status of work in progress

**For future you:**

-   Decision log entries integrated
-   Notes on what each file does
:::

##  {#biology-transition data-menu-title="Biology Transition"}

[Now: the biology of this week's activity]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
The activity you'll do with Nicole uses a real ecological dataset:

**California spiny lobster** (*Panulirus interruptus*)

-   Collected along the Santa Barbara Channel mainland coast
-   Santa Barbara Coastal Long-Term Ecological Research site
-   Tracks abundance, body size, and fishing pressure

**Why does this species matter?**
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#lobster-biology data-menu-title="Lobster Biology"}

[*Panulirus interruptus*: the basics]{.slide-title}

-   Spiny lobsters lack the large claws of their Atlantic cousins — they
    defend themselves with spines
-   Nocturnal foragers: urchins, mussels, snails, worms
-   **Keystone predators** in kelp forest ecosystems
-   Long-lived: can exceed 30 years
-   Commercially important: the largest US West Coast crustacean fishery
    by value

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#lobster-data data-menu-title="Lobster Data"}

**The measurement you'll work with:**

**Carapace length (mm)** The shell from the rostrum to the tail

Carapace length is a proxy for:

-   Age
-   Reproductive maturity
-   Ecological role

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#mpa-methods data-menu-title="MPA Methods"}

Methods:

The number and sizes of spiny lobster are recorded by divers in four 60
x 5 m (300 m2 total) lobster transects that are associated with each
permanent SBC LTER kelp forest community survey transect.

Data on the abundance and size of the California spiny lobster,
Panulirus interruptus,

-   collected annually in late summer

-   five sites (Arroyo Quemado, Carpinteria, Isla Vista, Mohawk and
    Naples)

Santa Barbara Coastal LTER, D. Reed, and R. Miller. 2022. SBC LTER:
Reef: Abundance, size and fishing effort for California Spiny Lobster
(Panulirus interruptus), ongoing since 2012 ver 8. Environmental Data
Initiative.
https://doi.org/10.6073/pasta/25aa371650a671bafad64dd25a39ee18 (Accessed
2026-04-13). ::: ---

##  {#mpa-context data-menu-title="MPA Context"}

[Why marine protected areas?]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
**Two of the five study sites are MPAs since 2012:**

-   **IVEE** — Isla Vista Reef
-   **NAPL** — Naples Reef

**Three sites are not protected:**

-   AQUE — Arroyo Quemado
-   CARP — Carpinteria
-   MOHK — Mohawk Reef

**The central question:** Does MPA protection change lobster abundance,
size, and the relationship between fishing pressure and population
structure?
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#fishing-pressure data-menu-title="Fishing Pressure"}

[Trap counts as a proxy for fishing pressure]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
The dataset has two components you'll analyze separately:

**Lobster abundance and size** (Owner's dataset)

-   Individual carapace measurements
-   Site, year, month

**Commercial trap buoy counts** (Collaborator's dataset)

-   Number of trap floats observed
-   Proxy for fishing effort / pressure

**Together:** you can ask how fishing pressure relates to lobster
population structure.
:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

##  {#why-this-matters data-menu-title="Why This Matters"}

[Connecting biology to your analysis]{.slide-title}

::: body-text
When you make analytical decisions in the activity, the biology matters:

-   Setting a size threshold at 70 mm — [California spiny
    lobsters](https://www.google.com/search?q=California+spiny+lobsters&rlz=1C5GCCM_enUS1118US1125&oq=reproductive+maturity+spiny+lobster&gs_lcrp=EgZjaHJvbWUyBggAEEUYOTIHCAEQIRigATIHCAIQIRigATIHCAMQIRigATIHCAQQIRirAtIBCDY5NzhqMGo3qAIIsAIB8QUHXffP1sm9cQ&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8&ved=2ahUKEwj6mL-p-emTAxUqIEQIHa_fA1IQgK4QegQIAxAC)
    may take 5–9 years to reach reproductive maturity, maturing around
    63.5–78.2 mm CL before they reach the legal harvesting size,
    ensuring they can breed at least once.
-   Filtering out NAPL — what are you losing ecologically?
-   The "high" fishing pressure threshold of ≥ 8 traps — what does that
    mean for the population?

**Data science without domain knowledge produces answers that don't mean
anything.**
:::
